name: Southern Samo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog sout2844 lists only Dwyer 1989/2006 subclassification notes; no phonology/grammar of Southern Samo (sbd) located online

new_statements.quote: San Maka is a tonal language with three level tones, designated, according to the IPA, by diacritics: acute (high), macron (mid) and grave (low). Vowel sequences may bear the following combinations of tones: level cv́v́; cv̄v̄; cv̀v̀ / falling cv́v̀; cv́v̄; cv̄v̀ / rising cv̀v́; cv̄v́. Susanne Platiel focused on distribution of tonal units according to the types of syllables and words. She showed that words of the CVCV structure cannot carry the mid tone in both syllables if they contain closed or semi-closed vowels: /i/, /u/, /e/, /o/ (Platiel 1974: 132). Platiel also pointed out the rarity of tonal minimal pairs and triplets
new_statements.citation: Perekhvalskaya, Elena. 2021. Grammatical functions of tone in San Maka. Mandenkan 65: 333-348. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.2574 (Section 2.1.5 Tonal system)
new_statements.locator: p. 336, section 2.1.5 'Tonal system' (same statement in Perekhvalskaya 2017, Mandenkan 57, p. 53, section 2.1.2)
new_statements.rule_in_words: San Maka (Southern Samo) is a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus contour combinations on vowel sequences); tone is lexically and grammatically distinctive. Neither of the two accessible modern descriptions (Perekhvalskaya 2017, 2021) mentions word stress, accent or metrical prominence at all; no statement about where stress falls exists in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (source is silent). Tonal restriction noted: CVCV words with close/half-close vowels cannot be M-M (Platiel 1974: 132).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone description; citation forms of nouns and verbs (neutral form is the dictionary form). Nothing on phrase-level prominence or intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Perekhvalskaya's 'San Maka' / 'Southern San (san-maka)' is the southern variety of the San/Samo cluster (Toma area, Nayala province), the same variety as Platiel's 'parler samo de Toma' and Ki's 'san du sud ou parler de Toma'; Glottolog files all of these under sout2844 Southern Samo [sbd]. Northern varieties (Matya stj, Maya sym) are separate languages with low mutual intelligibility. Glottolog's Daniel & Shaw 1977 'Samo phonemes' is Papua New Guinea Samo, misassigned.

sources.locator: p. 336, section 2.1.5 'Tonal system' (same statement in Perekhvalskaya 2017, Mandenkan 57, p. 53, section 2.1.2)
sources.note: Section 2.1 Phonology (pp. 334-337) covers vowels, consonants, floating nasal, vowel harmony and tonal system (2.1.5, p. 336: three level tones H/M/L, level/falling/rising combinations on vowel sequences, citing Platiel 1974: 132, 144). Nothing at all on stress, accent, metrical foot or prosodic word (the only 'foot' hits are body-part glosses).

sources.citation: Perekhvalskaya, Elena. 2017. Basic morphosyntax of verbal and non-verbal clauses in San-Maka. Mandenkan 57: 49-76. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.1070
